title: Build the Comment Bank Now, or Type the Same Note Forty Times in October
author: Doan Winkel
source: How to Teach With AI (howtoteachwithai.substack.com), August 20, 2026
summary: Doan Winkel offers a concrete, narrow AI workflow aimed at a specific and well-documented teacher problem: feedback quality degrading under grading fatigue late in a semester. His diagnosis is that the comments teachers repeat most often, on thesis clarity, citations, or circular conclusions, are also the ones that erode fastest into vague shorthand by the twenty-fifth repetition of a grading session. His proposed fix is to build a bank of roughly twelve polished, reusable comments in August, either by feeding an AI tool ten to twenty of last semester's actual comments to identify and sharpen repeated patterns, or by having AI draft comments from an assignment's prompt and rubric if no prior comments exist. Winkel is explicit that the bank must be rewritten in the teacher's own voice and that every banked comment requires one student-specific line before it goes out, arguing this ten-second addition is what separates a personalized comment from a canned one. The piece frames the entire exercise as a twenty-minute investment against a foreseeable and costly failure mode, uneven, exhausted feedback quality by the tenth week of the semester.
points: Winkel's key diagnostic insight is that the highest-value comments (those addressing universal, recurring mistakes) are also the ones most vulnerable to fatigue-driven degradation, since they get repeated most often within a single grading session.

His two-tier AI workflow is specific and reusable: extract patterns from a teacher's own prior comments when available, or generate a first draft from the assignment prompt and rubric when it isn't, in both cases with an explicit [add specific example] placeholder built in.

The 'one line' rule (one student-specific sentence appended to every banked comment) is his safeguard against the bank feeling automated, converting a roughly four-minute writing task into a ten-second personalization task without sacrificing the felt sense that 'a person read their work.'

He explicitly scopes the initial implementation to a single upcoming assignment rather than the whole course, reducing the activation barrier and giving teachers a real-world test of whether the bank holds up before committing more time to it.

The piece's 'Two Octobers' framing makes the intervention's stakes concrete by contrasting two versions of the same fatigued grading night, tying a twenty-minute August task directly to feedback equity between a class's first ten students and its last ten.
quotes: Fourth hour of grading. Assignment thirty-one. You type "your thesis is a topic, not an argument" for the twenty-fifth time, except by now it comes out as "unclear thesis, see me.
The comments we repeat most are the ones that matter most. We repeat them because the mistake is universal in our course. They also degrade fastest under fatigue.
Write each one well, one time, while you're calm and not staring down a stack. Then pull from that bank instead of retyping it at 11pm.
Every banked comment gets one line specific to that student before it goes out. The banked part carries the teaching. The one custom line makes a student feel like a person read their work.
Ten seconds instead of four minutes. The student gets the calm August version of your thinking, not the paper-thirty-one version.

You finish at midnight and you know the last ten students got less than the first ten. In the other, you paste, you add one line about paragraph three, and you're done in half the time. Every student gets the version you wrote when you were thinking clearly.
